title: Atomic oven with rapid thermal response for atom experiments
authors: Weilong Huang, Congjun Zou, Feiyu Dong, Huirong Xiao, Zejian Ren, Shanchao Zhang
abstract: Atomic oven generating controllable atomic beam flux plays a fundmental role in quantum gas experiments. Here, we report a new heater design that can heat up an high temperature atomic oven with fast thermal response. The new heater shows a heating rate improved by 7.65 times comparing to that of the onventional resistive heater while the crucible temperature can heated up to 1200K. With this oven, we generated a collimated ytterbium beam with flux exceeding $10^{14} \text{ atoms/s}$ at 823 K. We believe that our design offers a promising solution for shortening experimental dead time and improve the experiment efficiency in cold atom researches.
summary: The paper introduces an innovative inductive heating design for atomic ovens used in quantum physics experiments. This new heater significantly accelerates the temperature ramp-up time compared to conventional resistive heaters while maintaining high stability up to 1200 K. The resulting oven can generate highly collimated, high-flux atomic beams, promising to drastically improve efficiency in cold atom research.
main_problem: The slow thermal response time of conventional resistive heating methods used in atomic ovens significantly prolongs apparatus preparation time for quantum gas experiments.
main_result: A new inductive heater design was developed, achieving a 7.65-fold improvement in heating rate and enabling stable operation up to 1200 K while generating high-flux ytterbium beams.
method: The authors designed and tested an atomic oven using inductive heating via an AC driven copper coil, comparing its performance against traditional resistive heating methods.
model_or_system: The system is an atomic oven used to generate a controllable, collimated beam of atoms (e.g., Yb). The thermal dynamics are modeled using heat transfer equations ($ rac{C_p}{m} rac{dT}{dt} = P_{in} - P_{loss}$), and the control loop uses PI feedback.
key_observables: Atomic flux exceeding $10^{14} 	ext{ atoms/s}$, temperature stability ($\Delta T < \pm 2	ext{ K}$), and heating rate comparison (7.65x improvement).
important_parameters: Temperature range up to $1200	ext{ K}$; flux measurement at $823	ext{ K}$.
main_assumptions: The superior power transfer scaling of inductive coupling compared to contact-based resistive heating for refractory elements.
figures_summary: Figures compare time-resolved temperature evolution (resistive vs. inductive), show wide-range thermal setpoint programming, and display fluorescence spectroscopy confirming measured flux dependence on temperature.
paper_structure: The paper details the limitations of current ovens, introduces the inductive heating design based on theoretical modeling, presents experimental results comparing speed and stability against resistive methods, and concludes with measurements of high-flux atomic beams suitable for advanced quantum experiments.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses a critical engineering bottleneck (slow thermal response) in cold atom and quantum gas experiments, providing a robust platform necessary for increasing experimental uptime and repetition rates in AMO research.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Experimental setup of the inductively heated atomic source and optical detection system. A radio-frequency- driven copper induction coil surrounds the atomic crucible, while fluorescence and absorption of the atomic beam are probed downstream using a resonant laser. Inset: Schematic of the atomic crucible and collimating nozzle geometry. The crucible is machined from 304 stainless steel and optimized by balancing eddy current penetrating depth considerations and vacuum machining constraints. Key geometrical parameters, including crucible wall thickness and capillary dimensions, are indicated in units of millimeters (mm).

FIG. 2. Time-resolved temperature evolution of the atomic crucible under resistive heater (blue) and inductive heater (red), measured under identical geometrical configurations and target temperature (773 K). The time constants T1 and T2 represent the 10 %–90 % rise times, indicating the significantly faster thermal response of the inductive heating method.

FIG. 3. Wide-range thermal setpoint-programmed heating. Time-resolved temperature profiles demonstrating the sys- tem’s ability to rapidly reach and maintain precise target temperatures across an extensive range from 373 K to 1273 K. This confirms not only the fast thermal response but also the high maximum operating temperature and excellent long- term stability of the inductive heating setup.
